title: Pair Counter Across Two Lists
statement:
Build a structure over two integer lists: a short list small and a long list big. It supports two operations:

  • PairCounter(small, big) stores both lists.
  • bump(index, delta) adds delta to big[index]. Only big ever changes.
  • pairs(target) returns how many index pairs (i, j) have small[i] + big[j] === target. Pairs are counted by position, so equal values at different positions count separately.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first one creates the structure. The expected output has one entry per operation, null where nothing is returned.

examples.why: At first 1 + 4 and 2 + 3 (twice) make 5. After big[2] becomes 6, only the two 2 + 3 pairs remain.
big becomes [7, 7]. Both 5s pair with both 7s: 2 × 2 = 4 pairs. Counting distinct values would give 1.

constraints: At most 1000 calls each to bump and pairs
hints: Checking every (i, j) pair per query costs small.length × big.length. Which list is cheap to loop over?
Loop over the short list. For each small[i], you need to know how many positions of big hold target − small[i]. Keep that in a map from value to count.
On bump, the old value loses one count and the new value gains one. Keep a copy of big so you know the old value.

explain.intuition:
The two lists have very different sizes, and that is the whole point. A query can afford to touch every element of small (1000), but not every element of big (100 000), and certainly not every pair.

So keep big as a frequency map. A query walks small and asks the map how many entries equal target − small[i]. An update is a small move inside the map: the old value's count drops by one and the new value's count rises by one. It is the same trick as two-sum, kept alive across updates, much like a store that keeps derived counts in sync instead of recomputing them on every render.
steps: Store small, a copy of big, and a map count from each value in big to how many times it appears.
pairs(target): sum count[target − x] (0 if missing) over every x in small.
Optionally group small by value too, so repeated values are looked up once and multiplied.
pitfalls: Building the map over small and looping over big. Correct, but 100 times slower per query.
Forgetting to decrement the old value on bump, so stale values keep matching.
Counting distinct value pairs instead of index pairs; duplicates must multiply.

complexity.time: O(1) per bump, O(small.length) per pairs

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Store both lists; on each query test every (i, j) pair.
solutions.time: O(1) per bump, O(n₁·n₂) per pairs

solutions.title: Frequency map over the long list
solutions.idea: Keep counts of big's values; each query loops over the short list and looks up the complement.
solutions.time: O(1) per bump, O(n₁) per pairs

followups: Both lists can now be updated, and both are large. What would you trade?
Queries vastly outnumber updates and targets repeat. What could you cache, and when must the cache be cleared?
